title: Still Sharing API Docs in Word or PDF? Here's How to Move On
summary: Still emailing Word or PDF API docs? Move to private, interactive Theneo portals with customer-level access and an AI Agent that handles writing and cleanup.
body_markdown:
I was speaking with a team at an insurance company recently, and at some point I asked how they share their API documentation with partners.


‍


“We email it,” they said. “It's a Word file. Sometimes we send a PDF.”


‍


As we talked more, it became clear how much extra work this was creating for everyone involved.


‍


Partners would run into questions and email their account managers. Account managers would forward those questions to developers. Someone would eventually send back an explanation, sometimes with an updated document attached.


‍


And then the same thing would happen with the next partner.


‍


There was also the issue of keeping documentation up to date. Once you've sent a PDF to ten different partners, how do you make sure they're all working with the latest version?


‍


The interesting thing is that this isn't unusual. Plenty of established companies, particularly in industries like insurance, banking, and healthcare, still manage API documentation through Word files, PDFs, and email.


‍


And it makes sense how they got there. Word documents are easy to create, everyone knows how to use them, and emailing a file seems straightforward enough.


‍


Until you're managing multiple APIs, dozens of partners, and constant updates.


‍


At that point, the documentation itself becomes something your team has to spend time managing, rather than something that helps people integrate with your APIs.


‍


But moving away from Word and PDF doesn't have to mean rewriting your documentation or starting a complicated migration project.


‍


And putting the docs online doesn't mean making them public. You can give individual clients a private place to sign in and see only the API documentation you want to share with them.


‍


You can use the API information you already have to build **interactive API documentation** that partners can access from one place. And with tools like Theneo, getting started is much easier than building a documentation system yourself.


‍


Here's what actually changes when you make that switch, and how to get there without starting from scratch.


‍


## Where Word and PDF API documentation starts to get in the way


A Word document isn't a bad place to write down how an API works. The trouble starts when that document becomes the main way every partner learns about the API.


Every attachment is a snapshot. If an endpoint changes next week, the file you've already emailed won't change with it. And when a partner asks about an error code or a required field, someone on your team has to find the answer, explain it, and often update another copy of the document.


That usually shows up in a few familiar ways:


None of this means your team has been doing things wrong. It usually means a process that worked for a handful of partners hasn't kept pace with the number of people using your API.


## What changes when your API documentation becomes interactive?


**Interactive API documentation is a searchable online API reference where developers can read endpoint details and, when access is configured, test API requests from the same page.** Instead of passing around another attachment, you give partners a link to your documentation portal.


That one change is useful on its own. A partner knows where to find the published reference, and your team can update the central documentation instead of redistributing files.


But the bigger difference is what partners can do when they get there:


For a bank onboarding a fintech partner or an insurer working with new brokers, those small improvements can take a lot of avoidable back-and-forth out of the process.


## Keep API documentation private, with different access for every client


For an insurance company working with brokers or a bank onboarding fintech partners, a public API documentation site isn't always the answer. One partner may be approved to use a particular API while another needs access to a completely different set of endpoints.


Theneo's[private customer portals](https://docs.theneo.io/your-docs-site/private-customer-portal) let you give customers an authenticated, branded place to read the documentation intended for them. You can keep one centrally managed source of documentation while offering different approved views to different customers and individual users.


The important distinction is that **private doesn't have to mean static** . A client can have a searchable, interactive reference without being able to view documentation meant for another client. For a deeper look, see[how Theneo approaches private API documentation and granular access](https://www.theneo.io/blog/private-api-documentation-partners-ai-agents) .


## How to move API documentation from Word or PDF to Theneo


**The simplest approach is to reuse your existing API information, organize it into a structured reference, and publish it in Theneo.** You don't have to start by rewriting every page of your documentation.


### 1. Gather the files you already share


Start with the Word documents, PDFs, shared guides, and email attachments your partners actually use. If you also have an OpenAPI or Swagger specification, or a Postman collection, include that too.


You're looking for the technical information that's already there: endpoints, parameters, authentication steps, example requests and responses, and error codes. Don't wait until every file is perfectly organized before you begin.


### 2. Work out what can be imported and what needs structuring


If you have an OpenAPI specification or Postman collection, Theneo can import it and generate an editable API reference. This is the fastest starting point because the endpoint structure is already machine-readable.


If you only have Word files and PDFs, the technical details need to be organized into a structured API reference first. You can do that in Theneo's editor, and talk to the Theneo team about migration assistance if you want help planning the move.


That's worth distinguishing from a one-click file conversion: a PDF by itself doesn't guarantee that endpoint definitions, authentication details, and examples can be recovered accurately. The information is still useful, but it deserves a quick review as it becomes interactive.


### 3. Let Theneo's in-editor AI Agent do the writing and cleanup


Once the technical details are in your project, you don't have to fix every description manually. Open[Theneo's AI Agent inside the editor](https://docs.theneo.io/ai/ai-in-theneo/ai-co-pilot-technical-writer) , tell it what you need in plain English, and let it work through the documentation.

### 4. Publish a portal and share the link


Once the reference is ready, publish it as a hosted documentation portal. Your partners can open one link, browse the endpoints, and use the API explorer where you've enabled it.


Instead of repeatedly sending updated attachments, you maintain the published reference in one place. You can publish privately, invite specific customers, and give each of them the right level of access. For a walkthrough of the process, see[Theneo's migration guide](https://docs.theneo.io/get-started/migrate-to-theneo) .


## What actually changes when you stop sending PDF attachments?


The switch isn't just about how your documentation looks. It changes how partners find it, who can access it, and how much work your team does to maintain it.


## How long does migration take?


This depends much more on what you already have than on how many people are on your documentation team.


With a supported API specification or Postman collection, Theneo's import flow can get a project started quickly. You can then review the generated content, choose your branding, and publish.


Word- and PDF-only migrations take a little more preparation because those files may contain technical information without the structure needed for an interactive reference. A straightforward, well-documented API will be quicker to move than a complex one with missing endpoint details.


The important part is that **you don't need to treat migration as a months-long rewrite before you can see progress** . Start with a small, useful part of your API, publish it, then expand. If your documentation is scattered across folders and inboxes, ask the Theneo team to help you scope the first pass.


## Do you need an OpenAPI specification before you start?


**No. You can create and edit API documentation directly in Theneo.** An OpenAPI specification or Postman collection makes importing faster, but it isn't a requirement for building a documentation portal.


For companies whose reference exists only in Word or PDF, the practical first step is to organize the endpoint details you already have. If you later establish a supported API specification and connect a synchronization workflow, maintaining the docs can become easier still.


## What happens for partners once the docs are online?


Think back to the partner who needs to make their first API request.


Today they might receive a PDF, search for an endpoint, copy a sample into a separate testing tool, then email someone because the authentication example doesn't quite match what they see.


With interactive documentation, they can start at the portal, find the endpoint, inspect the required parameters, and use an API explorer to try the request when they've been given the appropriate access.


Some questions will still need a person. But far fewer should be about finding the right document or figuring out whether an attachment is current.


If you're improving the whole partner experience, this[guide to API documentation best practices](https://www.theneo.io/blog/api-documentation-best-practices-how-to-simplify-integration-for-developers) covers the details that help developers get to a successful first call.


## Keeping API documentation current after the move


A hosted portal solves the problem of scattered copies, but it doesn't automatically make every technical detail accurate forever. Someone still needs to keep the source of truth up to date.


Theneo supports API versioning, changelogs, and synchronization with supported specifications and development workflows. With the right setup, your team can reduce manual updates and give partners a clearer record of what's changed.


That matters in partner-heavy industries. When someone asks when a parameter became required, a maintained changelog and versioned reference are more useful than digging through old emails.


## You don't have to move everything at once


The insurance team I spoke with already had a lot of API information written down. Their challenge wasn't creating more content. It was giving partners a reliable way to use what the team had already produced.


If that's where your company is today, start small. Choose one API, collect the documentation your partners receive, and see what it would take to turn that information into a usable online reference.


You can keep improving your documentation as you go. What matters is getting out of the cycle of sending a new file every time someone needs an answer.
